title: Personal pronouns and αὐτός

objectives.can: Parse the forms of ἐγώ, σύ and αὐτός and say whom each refers to.

explanation.summary: Greek has a personal pronoun for 'I' (ἐγώ), one for 'you' (σύ), and for the third person it uses αὐτός. The first two have no gender; αὐτός has all three genders and takes three kinds of meaning depending on where it stands.

sections.heading: First and second person: ἐγώ and σύ
body: ἐγώ means 'I' in the singular and, with a different stem, 'we' (ἡμεῖς) in the plural. σύ means 'you' in the singular and 'you' (ὑμεῖς) in the plural. English uses one word for both numbers of 'you', so you have to watch the Greek form: σύ is one person, ὑμεῖς is more than one. These two pronouns have no gender, because the speaker and the person spoken to are clear from the situation.

The forms are listed below. Each of the singular forms has a short form and a longer one: μου, μοι, με beside ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ for 'I'; σου, σοι, σε beside σοῦ, σοί, σέ for 'you'. The short forms are the ordinary ones. The long forms are used for emphasis and are common after prepositions. A short form can take an accent in some positions, as a matter of the rules for unaccented (enclitic) words, so you will also meet μού, μοί and σού, σοί; these are the same words.

Because the Greek verb already shows person and number, the nominative pronoun is not needed for the sense. When it is there, it usually adds emphasis or contrast. In John 21:17 Peter says σὺ οἶδας, σὺ γινώσκεις: the repeated σύ stresses that Jesus is the one who knows.

sections.heading: The pronoun's cases
body: The oblique cases (all but the nominative) are used just as for nouns. The genitive often shows possession: where English says 'my', 'your', Greek puts the genitive of the pronoun after the noun, as in τὴν ψυχήν μου or τὸ ὄνομα σου. The dative marks the person receiving or affected: δός μοι, 'give to me'. The accusative gives the object: φιλεῖς με, 'you love me'.

sections.heading: The third person: αὐτός, αὐτή, αὐτό
body: Greek has no separate third-person pronoun for 'he, she, it' in the nominative. In the other cases, the forms of αὐτός do that work: αὐτοῦ 'of him, his', αὐτῷ 'to him', αὐτόν 'him', αὐτῆς 'of her, her', αὐτῶν 'of them, their'. It is one of the commonest words in the New Testament. Its gender and number agree with the word it stands for; its case comes from its own job in its own clause.

αὐτός has three kinds of use, which are told apart by position. (1) On its own, in the genitive, dative or accusative, it means 'him, her, it, them', as in ἔλαβον αὐτόν (John 1:12), 'they received him'. (2) In the 'predicate position', that is, before the article and noun, or after them with no repeated article, it means 'himself, itself': αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος in 1 Thessalonians 4:16, 'the Lord himself'; αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα in Romans 8:16, 'the Spirit itself'. (3) In the attributive position, after the article, it means 'the same': ὁ αὐτός in Hebrews 13:8, and τὸ αὐτό and τῷ αὐτῷ in 1 Corinthians 1:10.
The nominative forms αὐτός, αὐτή, αὐτό therefore usually mean 'himself, herself, itself' (the emphatic use); they are rarely used for plain 'he'.

sections.heading: A note on the labels in the corpus
body: The analysed text labels αὐτός as a pronoun when it means 'him', 'himself' and so on, and as an adjective when it means 'the same'. This is a reasonable choice, because in the 'same' use it stands inside the article–noun group like an adjective. The case, number and gender are the same either way.

misunderstandings: αὐτός does not mean 'he' in the nominative as a rule. As a subject it usually means 'himself' or marks emphasis; for plain 'he' the verb ending is enough.
σύ and ὑμεῖς are both 'you' in English but not in Greek: σύ addresses one person, ὑμεῖς several. Check the number before you translate.
Some forms of αὐτός are shared by two genders: αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ and αὐτῶν can be masculine or neuter, and αὐτῶν can also be feminine. Look at what the pronoun stands for.
The longer forms ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ are not different words from μου, μοι, με; they are the stressed forms of the same pronoun.

deeper.heading: Why the third person has no pronoun of its own
body: Greek grammarians usually explain the gap by history: the old third-person pronoun went out of ordinary use and the intensive pronoun αὐτός moved into its place in the oblique cases. The explanation is a view of the history; for reading you only need to know how the forms are used in the New Testament.

examples.analysis: με is the accusative singular of ἐγώ, the object of φιλεῖς: 'do you love me?'. σὺ is the nominative of σύ, repeated for emphasis (the verbs already say 'you'). σε is the accusative of σύ: Peter's 'I love you'. Notice that the same pair of forms changes meaning with the speaker.

examples.analysis: αὐτόν is accusative singular masculine, 'him': the object of ἔλαβον. αὐτοῖς is dative plural masculine, 'to them'. αὐτοῦ is genitive singular masculine and shows possession: 'his name'. This is the ordinary third-person use.

check.explain: αὐτός stands after the article, the attributive position, so it means 'the same'. It is nominative singular masculine, agreeing with Ἰησοῦς Χριστός.

reading.why: Three short exchanges between Jesus and Peter in which με, σε, σύ and αὐτῷ occur in plain speech: a good place to see the first- and second-person pronouns in use.
